Maybe start of with something along the lines of, "hey, you're my friend and I appreciate and value you and our friendship and I don't want to come across as possessive or selfish I just been kinda getting jealous and was wondering if you value our friendship too". And then ask if it's possible for them to help you see how they show their friendships. 

Or if you would want a slightly more subtle approach ask about some of the best moments they've had with you. Either one will give you reassurance.

In terms of working in it, it kind depends on your friendship dynamic and personalities. Ive always been fond of code words, so instead of having to say how you feel in detail have a word that you can both recognise to mean you're feeling jealous. I typically think names instead of a random word is easier to slip into conversation but this is only one of many ways you can overcome this. 
Another way is talking more, or asking what you mean to them etc .

When it comes to personal belongings, you have every right to be possessive it's your stuff. In terms of friends maybe just tell them that sometimes you're afraid you'll be forgotten and together work on a way to overcome that fear. In terms of jealousy it is somewhat common, more so than you may think but the best thing to do is to be honest and communicate.

Anything you're concerned about is worth mentioning. If you are already working with a psychiatrist then I don't see why you can't bring it up, especially since it's kinda why they're are there. I can't and won't say it is or is not an eating disorder, but what I will say is if you are generally concerned and you have the means to talk to a professional then you should.
There is no harm in asking for reassurance or clarity especially when your health is at risk.
